title: Cybersecurity Is Every Leader's Job
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The piece argues that cybersecurity is a leadership responsibility, not something to hand off to the IT department. Most modern attacks start with persuading a person, through a fake urgent email from the CEO, a spoofed help desk call or an invoice with new banking details, so every leader who directs people or controls a budget plays a security role. The author frames security as stewardship, since people trust leaders with their livelihoods, personal information and reputations. He then gives three leadership moves: model good habits because teams watch what leaders do rather than what policy says, make it safe to report mistakes within minutes, and build processes that do not depend on any one person, such as two approvals for large payments and a second-channel check on account changes. Security is presented as a set of risk choices that belong at the leadership table, and as a competency for all leaders rather than a technical specialty. The post is short, about 500 words, and closes with a prompt to examine where your organization needs more judgment.
points: Because many attacks exploit human trust rather than code, every leader who directs people or controls a budget is already part of the security perimeter.
Leaders teach by example: sharing passwords or skipping multi-factor authentication signals that convenience beats protection, while verifying unusual requests makes caution a mark of judgment.
Making it safe to report a clicked bad link within minutes turns a possible breach into a contained incident; blame drives people to hide mistakes.
Resilient processes beat heroic individuals: two approvals on large payments, second-channel confirmation of banking changes, and access that ends when a role ends.
What data to hold, for how long, who can access it and which vendors to trust are risk decisions that belong to leaders, not only to IT.
quotes: Too many organizations still treat cybersecurity as something only the IT department handles. That framing is convenient but dead wrong.

People trust leaders with their livelihoods, their personal information, and their reputations. Protecting that trust cannot be handed off entirely to specialists, any more than integrity can be relegated to the legal department.
Team members pay closer attention to what leaders do than to what policy says.
The team member who clicks a bad link and says so within minutes is an asset, not a problem child. The one who hides it for fear of blame can turn an incident into a serious breach.
Security is, and always has been, a set of choices about risk, and those choices belong at the leadership table, not solely with IT.
They require two approvals for large payments, confirm any change in account details through a second channel, and ensure access ends when a role ends.
Attackers count on busy people who trust too quickly and leaders who assume someone else is watching.
